newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai Premier hopefuls declare on Burma rights.
newsitem.headline: Thai Premier hopefuls declare on Burma rights.

text.p: Thai prime ministerial hopefuls Chuan Leekpai and Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said on Wednesday they would allow human rights groups to hold protests here against Rangoon's crackdown on democracy activities in Burma.
Chuan and Chavalit, frontrunners to lead a coalition government after November 17 polls, said if elected they both would strive to persuade Burma to improve its human rights record.

Chuan, prime minister in 1992-1995, said in a televised debate with his rival that the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) should review Burma's human rights performance before granting Rangoon membership in the regional group.
ASEAN groups Thailand with Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei and Vietnam.

Chuan said if elected, he would try to maintain Thailand's policy of constructive engagement toward Burma. He said Bangkok should continue balancing its national interests of maintaining friendly relations with Burma without ignoring human rights violation by its neighbour.
Defence Minister Chavalit said he also would not obstruct Thai activist groups holding rallies here in support of Burmese democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
But the former army chief said Thailand should focus on persuading the Burmese military government to heed international calls for improving its human rights performance.
Burma's military rulers have come under steady international criticism over their human rights policy. They in recent months detained and then released hundreds of Suu Kyi's supporters.
Chuan's Democrat Party and Chavalit's New Aspiration Party are expected to each win 120-130 seats in Thailand's new 393-seat lower House of Representatives on Sunday.

Touching on Thai election issues, Chavalit denied suggestions by his critics that he favoured big military spending but he said there was room for Thailand to trim its growing national coffers of over 300 billion baht ($12 billion).

He said large government surplus funds, a product of eight consecutive years of fiscal surpluses, should be partly invested by the public sector to offset a slowdown of the Thai economy this year. He did not elaborate.
The Thai economy is projected to expand about seven percent in 1996, its slowest pace in 10 years.
